title: Easy beats heroic
hook: the famous willpower-drain effect failed a large 2016 replication (Hagger et al.)

segments.voice: Yesterday: after the kettle. Did your cue come this morning, and did the practice follow it, even for thirty seconds? Day three hundred twelve.

Picture a lab in the late 1990s. A plate of warm chocolate chip cookies sits on a table, next to a bowl of radishes. Some hungry volunteers are allowed the cookies. Others are told: radishes only, please. Then everyone gets an impossible puzzle. The radish group, who had spent their self-control resisting the cookies, gave up sooner. The idea that grew from this was simple and everywhere: willpower is a tank of fuel, and every time you resist something, the tank runs lower. Hundreds of studies followed. Then, in 2016, two dozen labs tried it again, carefully, all at once. Today: easy beats heroic.
screen: `COOKIES OR RADISHES.` → `WILLPOWER AS A FUEL TANK.` → `TWO DOZEN LABS TRY AGAIN.`

segments.voice: First, what happened. The 2016 project, led by Martin Hagger with labs across several countries, ran one agreed version of a classic willpower test, two tasks back to back rather than the cookies, on more than two thousand people. The draining effect came out close to zero. Other researchers have argued about the method, and the debate isn't fully closed, but the neat picture of a willpower tank running dry is much shakier than the posters say. Remember compared to what. Second, what that frees you from. If willpower isn't a tank, then struggling isn't proof that yours is small. And here's a finding that points somewhere useful. Several studies suggest that people who seem to have lots of self-control don't spend their days resisting temptation heroically. They meet fewer temptations. They've set things up so the good thing is easy and the other thing is a little further away. Their habits do the work. Third, the old wisdom. The Tao Te Ching, the Chinese classic, has a word for acting without forcing: wu wei. We met it with the swimmer at the falls, who went in with the whirl and came out with the swirl. The book advises doing the hard thing while it's still easy, and the great thing while it's still small. Epictetus said something close from the Stoic side: start with small things, a little spilled oil, a little stolen wine, and practice there. Fourth, the Tuesday version. Heroic plans feel wonderful at night and collapse by Thursday. An hour of meditation, every day, starting tomorrow. Easy plans look almost silly: two minutes, after the kettle, cushion already on the floor. Silly wins. Make the practice so easy you'd feel odd skipping it.
screen: `THE FUEL TANK DIDN'T REPLICATE.` · `SET THINGS UP, DON'T WHITE-KNUCKLE.` · `WU WEI: ACT WITHOUT FORCING.` · `SILLY-EASY WINS BY THURSDAY.` · then, large: `EASY BEATS HEROIC.`

segments.voice: Take the practice you tied to your cue yesterday. Now make it easier. Shorter? Maybe one minute instead of five. Closer? Leave the cushion or the chair where you'll trip over it. Fewer steps? Put the note on the kettle itself. Pick one change that removes one bit of friction. Then sit, and notice how it feels to plan without clenching. The bell holds the time.
Easy beats heroic. Don't rely on a willpower tank; make the good thing easy and let habit carry it. Wu wei, acting without forcing. Today's word.
Your line: easy beats heroic. Before bed tonight, set up tomorrow's practice so it's already half done: the chair out, the note on the kettle, the phone in another room. Day three hundred twelve.

howItsDone: People who keep a daily practice often make it small and set it up in advance, like leaving a cushion out or keeping the session to two minutes, rather than relying on willpower each day.

original.note: Chinese: literally not-doing; action without forcing, a key idea of the Tao Te Ching.

trapdoor: what you thought: easy means lazy.
what it means: set things up so the good thing needs little effort, and habit carries it.
what a scholar hears: Hagger et al.'s 2016 registered replication of ego depletion, 23 labs, an effect near zero.

notes: Hagger et al. 2016: 23 labs, 2,141 participants, effect size near zero (d ≈ 0.04). Critics (including Baumeister) disputed the task used; the script says the debate isn't fully closed. Confirm.
Baumeister 1998 radish/cookie study: confirm details (hungry participants, unsolvable puzzles, radish group persisted less).
'People with high self-control meet fewer temptations': Hofmann et al. 2012 and Galla and Duckworth 2015; kept vague as 'several studies suggest'. Confirm.
Tao Te Ching 63 paraphrased (plan the difficult while it is easy; do the great while it is small). Enchiridion 12 paraphrased (begin with small things: spilled oil, stolen wine). Confirm both.
Callback to day 56, 'The swimmer at the falls' (Zhuangzi 19), where wu wei was the word.
Audit 2026-09-30: the teach no longer implies the 2016 replication repeated the cookie-and-radish study; it used a different two-task procedure (a letter-crossing task). Confirm.
